h: Trebuchets, towers and Loch Ness cruises
p: Before you head down to the ruins, the visitor centre has a short film that sets the scene, and when it ends there's a big reveal of the castle through the window. It's a lovely touch, so don't skip it. Then follow the path down to the water's edge.

Once you're among the ruins, look out for the full-size replica trebuchet, a siege engine of the kind used to attack castles like this one. It's a big hit with kids. The Grant Tower is the best-preserved part of the castle, and climbing its narrow stairs rewards you with a cracking view up and down the loch. Keep your eyes peeled for Nessie while you're up there; you never know.

Urquhart is one of Scotland's most popular sights, and it gets busy, especially when the tour coaches arrive. Going early in the day or later in the afternoon is calmer. Allow around two hours, and wear sturdy shoes, because the path down to the ruins is steep. The weather on the loch can change fast, so bring a waterproof.

Boat trips run on Loch Ness, some of them stopping at the castle, which gives you an amazing view from the water. Nearby Drumnadrochit has places to eat and visitor attractions dedicated to the Loch Ness mystery. Further south down the A82, Fort Augustus is a lovely spot to watch boats work their way up the Caledonian Canal's flight of locks, while Inverness is a short drive north.
